claim: The proportion of MDR-TB among new TB-patients in Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan increased from 13% in 2001 to 23% in 2014.
source: In this high MDR-TB incidence setting, the proportion of MDR-TB among new TB-patients increased from 13% in 2001 to 23% in 2014 despite the local introduction of the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended DOTS strategy in 1998 and an initially limited MDR-TB treatment program in 2003 (Cox et al., 2007; Ulmasova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2007 and Ulmasova et al., 2013, which provide the data for these proportions.

claim: The WHO recommended DOTS strategy was introduced in Karakalpakstan in 1998.
source: In this high MDR-TB incidence setting, the proportion of MDR-TB among new TB-patients increased from 13% in 2001 to 23% in 2014 despite the local introduction of the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended DOTS strategy in 1998 and an initially limited MDR-TB treatment program in 2003 (Cox et al., 2007; Ulmasova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2007 and Ulmasova et al., 2013.

claim: An initially limited MDR-TB treatment program was introduced in Karakalpakstan in 2003.
source: In this high MDR-TB incidence setting, the proportion of MDR-TB among new TB-patients increased from 13% in 2001 to 23% in 2014 despite the local introduction of the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended DOTS strategy in 1998 and an initially limited MDR-TB treatment program in 2003 (Cox et al., 2007; Ulmasova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2007 and Ulmasova et al., 2013.

claim: Combined resistance to all five first-line drugs was significantly greater in cohort 2 (47%) compared to cohort 1 (14%).
source: While the majority of strains from both cohorts were phenotypically resistant to additional first-line TB drugs (i.e. beyond rifampicin and isoniazid), combined resistance to all five first-line drugs was significantly greater in cohort 2 (47% in cohort 2 compared to 14% in cohort 1, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript with statistical significance (p<0.0001).

claim: Resistance to capreomycin was significantly greater in cohort 2 (23%) compared to cohort 1 (2%).
source: The same was true for resistance to the second-line injectable drug capreomycin (23% in cohort 2 compared to 2% in cohort 1, p=0.0001) (Appendix—table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript with statistical significance (p=0.0001).

claim: The higher rate of resistance to capreomycin in cohort 2 was attributable to primary resistance (infection by already resistant strains).
source: This finding was surprising as the isolates from cohort two patients - who were treated with individualized second-line regimens predominately comprising ofloxacin as the fluoroquinolone and capreomycin as the second-line injectable - were all obtained before the initiation of their treatment. In addition, there was no formal MDR-TB treatment program in Karakalpakstan prior to 2003. These elements imply that the higher rate of resistance to capreomycin was attributable to infection by already resistant strains (i.e. to primary resistance).
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the timing of sample collection and the absence of prior MDR-TB treatment programs.

claim: 6979 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) plus 537 variants located in 28 genes and upstream regions associated with drug resistance and bacterial fitness were determined using whole genome sequencing.
source: Utilizing WGS, we determined 6979 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) plus 537 variants located in 28 genes and upstream regions associated with drug resistance and bacterial fitness (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data obtained from whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: A dominant clade termed Central Asian Outbreak (CAO) comprised 173/277 (62.5%) closely related isolates within MTBC lineage 2 (Beijing-genotype).
source: The corresponding phylogeny revealed a dominant clade comprising 173/277 (62.5%) closely related isolates within MTBC lineage 2 (particularly Beijing-genotype) (Figure 1). This group, termed Central Asian Outbreak (CAO), showed a highly restricted genetic diversity (median pairwise distance of 21 SNPs, IQR 13–25) and was differentiated from a set of more diverse isolates by 38 specific SNPs (Appendix—figure 1, Supplementary file 1 ).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data and Figure 1.

claim: The CAO clade showed a highly restricted genetic diversity with a median pairwise distance of 21 SNPs (IQR 13–25).
source: This group, termed Central Asian Outbreak (CAO), showed a highly restricted genetic diversity (median pairwise distance of 21 SNPs, IQR 13–25) and was differentiated from a set of more diverse isolates by 38 specific SNPs (Appendix—figure 1, Supplementary file 1 ).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic distance analysis data.

claim: The CAO clade was differentiated from other isolates by 38 specific SNPs.
source: This group, termed Central Asian Outbreak (CAO), showed a highly restricted genetic diversity (median pairwise distance of 21 SNPs, IQR 13–25) and was differentiated from a set of more diverse isolates by 38 specific SNPs (Appendix—figure 1, Supplementary file 1 ).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: The proportion of CAO-isolates increased from 49% in 2001-2002 and 52% in 2003-2004 to 76% in 2005-06.
source: The proportion of CAO-isolates was similar between 2001–2002 and 2003–2004 (49% and 52%, respectively), but increased to 76% in 2005–06 (p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal data with statistical significance (p<0.01).

claim: 96.0% (166/173) of all Beijing-CAO isolates were associated with recent transmission (transmission index ≥1).
source: Beijing-CAO-isolates formed particularly large transmission networks (>50 patients; Figure 1); 96.0% (166/173) of all Beijing-CAO isolates were associated with recent transmission (i.e. transmission index ≥1), versus 48.4% (31/64) of non-CAO Beijing isolates (p<0.0001) and 57.5% (23/40) of non-Beijing isolates (p<0.0001) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission network analysis data with statistical significance.

claim: 48.4% (31/64) of non-CAO Beijing isolates were associated with recent transmission.
source: Beijing-CAO-isolates formed particularly large transmission networks (>50 patients; Figure 1); 96.0% (166/173) of all Beijing-CAO isolates were associated with recent transmission (i.e. transmission index ≥1), versus 48.4% (31/64) of non-CAO Beijing isolates (p<0.0001) and 57.5% (23/40) of non-Beijing isolates (p<0.0001) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission network analysis data.

claim: 57.5% (23/40) of non-Beijing isolates were associated with recent transmission.
source: Beijing-CAO-isolates formed particularly large transmission networks (>50 patients; Figure 1); 96.0% (166/173) of all Beijing-CAO isolates were associated with recent transmission (i.e. transmission index ≥1), versus 48.4% (31/64) of non-CAO Beijing isolates (p<0.0001) and 57.5% (23/40) of non-Beijing isolates (p<0.0001) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission network analysis data.

claim: The large CAO transmission network exhibited higher levels of drug resistance relative to non-Beijing strains.
source: In addition, the large CAO transmission network exhibited higher levels of drug resistance relative to non-Beijing strains, as reflected by the larger number of drugs for which phenotypic (p=0.0079) and genotypic drug resistance (p=0.0048) was detected Appendix—figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug resistance data with statistical significance.

claim: The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the CAO-clade emerged around 1974 (95% HPD 1969–1982).
source: Employing the Bayesian skyline model with a strict molecular clock set to 0.94 × 10−7 (s/s/y) specifically we determined that the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the CAO-clade emerged around 1974 (95% highest posterior density (HPD) 1969–1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by Bayesian phylogenetic analysis with specified confidence intervals.

claim: The mutation rate for the CAO clade was estimated at 0.94 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year (95% HPD 0.72–1.15 × 10−7).
source: Mutation rate estimates (under a relaxed clock model) ranged on average from 0.88 to 0.96 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year (s/s/y), depending on the demographic model, in favor for the Bayesian skyline model with a mutation rate of 0.94 × 10−7 (s/s/y) (95% HPD 0.72–1.15 × 10−7 (s/s/y)) (Appendix—table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Bayesian phylogenetic analysis with specified confidence intervals.

claim: The MRCA of the CAO-clade already exhibited a streptomycin resistance mutation (rpsL K43R).
source: The MRCA already exhibited a streptomycin resistance mutation (rpsL K43R) (Figure 2), and acquired isoniazid resistance (katG S315T) in 1977 (95% HPD 1973 – 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic reconstruction data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The CAO-clade acquired isoniazid resistance (katG S315T) in 1977 (95% HPD 1973 – 1983).
source: The MRCA already exhibited a streptomycin resistance mutation (rpsL K43R) (Figure 2), and acquired isoniazid resistance (katG S315T) in 1977 (95% HPD 1973 – 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: The most frequent CAO-clone acquired ethambutol and ethionamide resistance mutations (embB M306V, ethA T314I) around 1984 (95% HPD 1982–1989).
source: As an illustration, the most frequent CAO-clone (upper clade in Figure 2) acquired ethambutol and ethionamide resistance mutations (embB M306V, ethA T314I) around 1984 (95% HPD 1982–1989), and an MDR-genotype (rpoB S450L) around 1986 (95% HPD 1985–1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: The most frequent CAO-clone acquired an MDR-genotype (rpoB S450L) around 1986 (95% HPD 1985–1992).
source: As an illustration, the most frequent CAO-clone (upper clade in Figure 2) acquired ethambutol and ethionamide resistance mutations (embB M306V, ethA T314I) around 1984 (95% HPD 1982–1989), and an MDR-genotype (rpoB S450L) around 1986 (95% HPD 1985–1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: Fixation of mutations in the ribD promoter region and rpoC N698S occurred around 1990 (95% HPD 1989–1994).
source: The effective population size reached a plateau before fixation of mutations in the ribD promoter region (leading to para-aminosalicylic acid resistance) and rpoC N698S, putatively enhancing its fitness around 1990 (95% HPD 1989–1994) (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: Independent fixation of pyrazinamide (pncA Q10P and I133T) and kanamycin (eis −12 g/a) resistance-associated mutations was detected in 1992 and 1991 (both with 95% HPD rounded to 1991–1996).
source: Independent fixation of pyrazinamide (pncA Q10P and I133T) and kanamycin (eis −12 g/a) resistance-associated mutations was detected in 1992 and 1991 (both with 95% HPD rounded to 1991–1996) (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: 62.1% (172/277) of all MDR-MTBC isolates carried putative compensatory mutations in rpoA (n = 7), rpoC (n = 126) and rpoB (n = 43).
source: Overall, 62.1% (172/277) of all MDR-MTBC isolates carried putative compensatory mutations (Comas et al., 2012; Casali et al., 2014a) in rpoA (n = 7), rpoC (n = 126) and rpoB (n = 43) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data with citations to previous work defining compensatory mutations.

claim: Only 4/172 isolates harbored variants in more than one RNA polymerase-encoding gene.
source: These mutations were almost completely mutually exclusive, as only 4/172 isolates harbored variants in more than one RNA polymerase-encoding gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: CAO-isolates had more rpoC variants (56%) compared to other non-outbreak Beijing isolates (28%).
source: While mutations in rpoA and rpoB were equally distributed between Beijing-CAO isolates and other non-outbreak Beijing isolates, CAO-isolates had more rpoC variants (56% vs 28%, p=0.003) (Appendix—table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis with statistical significance (p=0.003).

claim: The mutation rpoC N698N accounted for 79/124 (63.7%) of CAO isolates with putative compensatory effects.
source: The mutation rpoC N698N accounted for 79/124 (63.7%) of CAO isolates with putative compensatory effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: The mean number of resistance mutations was higher among isolates carrying compensatory mutations (4.77) compared to those without (3.35).
source: The mean number of resistance mutations was higher among isolates carrying compensatory mutations (Figure 3A), 4.77 vs 3.35 mutations (two-sample t-test p=1.2×10−10).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with high significance (p=1.2×10−10).

claim: Isolates with compensatory mutations showed larger transmission indexes (37.16) than isolates presenting no compensatory mutation (9.22).
source: Notably, isolates with compensatory mutations also showed larger transmission indexes than isolates presenting no compensatory mutation, 37.16 vs 9.22 (Welch two-sample t-test p<2.2×10−16) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with high significance (p<2.2×10−16).

claim: CAO-isolates with compensatory mutations had more resistance-conferring mutations than CAO-isolates lacking such mutation.
source: CAO-isolates with compensatory mutations also had more resistance-conferring mutations than CAO-isolates lacking such mutation (ANOVA, Tukey multiple comparisons of means P adj = 0.0000012).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with high significance (P adj = 0.0000012).

claim: There was no difference observed for the means of resistance-conferring mutations among non-CAO isolates with or without compensatory mutations.
source: There was no difference observed for the means of resistance-conferring mutations among non-CAO isolates; compensatory mutation present vs. absent (P adj = 0.1978623) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference (P adj = 0.1978623).

claim: The presence of compensatory mutations was strongly associated with cluster sizes independent of the accumulation of resistance mutations in the Beijing-CAO clade.
source: Regression-based analyses of transmission success scores in the Beijing-CAO clade confirmed that the presence of compensatory mutations was strongly associated with cluster sizes independent of the accumulation of resistance mutations (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The association between compensatory mutations and transmission success was mostly observed for clusters initiated in the late 1980s and the 1990s.
source: This pattern was mostly observed for clusters initiated in the late 1980s and the 1990s.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of transmission patterns.

claim: Beijing-CAO isolates accounted for the third largest clade in Samara.
source: This analysis showed that Beijing-CAO isolates accounted for the third largest clade in Samara (Casali et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis with citation to Casali et al., 2014a.

claim: Three major Beijing outbreak clades (A, B, and CAO) accounted for 69.6% (491/705) of the MDR-TB cases in both Samara and Karakalpakstan.
source: Considering a third Beijing clade (termed clade A) restricted to Samara (Casali et al., 2014a), three major Beijing outbreak clades accounted for 69.6% (491/705) of the MDR-TB cases in both regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by combined phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: The three Beijing clades (A, B, and CAO) had more drug resistance conferring mutations with means of 5.0 (SEM 0.07), 4.2 (SEM 0.18), and 4.7 (SEM 0.11), respectively, compared to 3.6 (SEM 0.20) for other Beijing isolates.
source: The three Beijing clades (A, B, and CAO) in Samara and Karakalpakstan had more drug resistance conferring mutations (in addition to isoniazid and rifampicin resistance) with means of 5.0 (SEM 0.07), 4.2 (SEM 0.18), and 4.7 (SEM 0.11), respectively (Appendix—figure 5), than compared to only 3.6 (SEM 0.20) additional genotypic drug resistances (p<0.0001, p=0.0143, p<0.0001) for other Beijing isolates in both settings.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Isolates belonging to other MTBC genotypes (mainly lineage four clades) had a mean of 2.6 (SEM 0.20) additional drug resistance mediating mutations, lower than any Beijing-associated group.
source: Isolates belonging to other MTBC genotypes (mainly lineage four clades) were found with a mean of 2.6 (SEM 0.20) additional drug resistance mediating mutations, lower than any Beijing-associated group (p≤0.0009) (Appendix—figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis with statistical significance (p≤0.0009).

claim: MDR-MTBC isolates from Samara with compensatory mutations accumulated more resistance-associated mutations (4.57) compared to isolates lacking compensatory mutations (2.30).
source: Similar to Karakalpakstan, MDR-MTBC isolates from Samara with compensatory mutations also accumulated more resistance-associated mutations (4.57 vs 2.30 mutations per genome; two-sample t-test p<2.2×10−16) and had higher transmission indexes (50.32 vs 0.46; Welch two-sample t-test p<2.2×10−16) compared to isolates lacking compensatory mutations (Appendix—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with high significance (p<2.2×10−16).

claim: MDR-MTBC isolates from Samara with compensatory mutations had higher transmission indexes (50.32) compared to isolates lacking compensatory mutations (0.46).
source: Similar to Karakalpakstan, MDR-MTBC isolates from Samara with compensatory mutations also accumulated more resistance-associated mutations (4.57 vs 2.30 mutations per genome; two-sample t-test p<2.2×10−16) and had higher transmission indexes (50.32 vs 0.46; Welch two-sample t-test p<2.2×10−16) compared to isolates lacking compensatory mutations (Appendix—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with high significance (p<2.2×10−16).

claim: The presence of compensatory mutations, but not the accumulation of resistance mutations, was significantly and independently associated with network size in Beijing-A clade clusters originating in the 1980s and 1990s.
source: The impact of resistance conferring and compensatory mutations on the transmission success score in Beijing-A clade from Samara (Appendix—figure 7) was strikingly similar to the one observed in CAO isolates from Karakalpakstan. The presence of compensatory mutations, but not the accumulation of resistance mutations, was significantly and independently associated with network size in clusters originating in the 1980s and 1990s, with a maximum influence found in clusters starting in the late 1990s.
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis comparing Beijing-A and CAO clades.

claim: The proportions of isolates with pre-XDR and XDR resistance profiles among the three major Beijing clades were: clade A 96%, clade B 62%, clade CAO 50%.
source: Critically, the high proportions of isolates detected in both settings with pre-XDR and XDR resistance profiles among the three major Beijing clades (clade A, 96%; clade B, 62%; clade CAO, 50%; Appendix—table 4, Figure 6) reveal the low proportion of patients that are or would be eligible to receive the newly WHO endorsed short MDR-TB regimen.
evidence: The claim is supported by resistance profile analysis data.

claim: Only 0.5% (1/191) of patients in Karakalpakstan infected with Beijing clade A, B or CAO strains would benefit from the WHO short MDR-TB regimen.
source: As per definition of the WHO exclusion criteria, for example any confirmed or suspected resistance to one drug (except isoniazid) in the short regimen, only 0.5% (1/191 in Karakalpakstan) and 2.7% (8/300 in Samara) of the patients infected with either a Beijing clade A, B or CAO strain would benefit from a shortened MDR-TB therapy (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of resistance profiles against WHO eligibility criteria.

claim: Only 2.7% (8/300) of patients in Samara infected with Beijing clade A, B or CAO strains would benefit from the WHO short MDR-TB regimen.
source: As per definition of the WHO exclusion criteria, for example any confirmed or suspected resistance to one drug (except isoniazid) in the short regimen, only 0.5% (1/191 in Karakalpakstan) and 2.7% (8/300 in Samara) of the patients infected with either a Beijing clade A, B or CAO strain would benefit from a shortened MDR-TB therapy (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of resistance profiles against WHO eligibility criteria.

claim: Barely 20% of the estimated annual 480,000 new MDR-TB patients have access to adequate second-line treatment regimens.
source: Barely 20% of the estimated annual 480,000 new MDR-TB patients have access to adequate second-line treatment regimens.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about global MDR-TB treatment access.

claim: The majority of undiagnosed or ineffectively treated MDR-TB patients continue to transmit their infection and suffer high mortality.
source: The majority of undiagnosed or ineffectively treated MDR-TB patients continue to transmit their infection and suffer high mortality (WHO, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to WHO, 2016.

claim: The acquisition of drug resistance could lead to reduced bacterial fitness.
source: Based on early observations that the acquisition of drug resistance could lead to reduced bacterial fitness (Middlebrook and Cohn, 1953), it was hypothesized that drug-resistant MTBC-strains had a reduced capacity to transmit, and would not widely disseminate in the general population (Borrell and Gagneux, 2009; Billington et al., 1999; Burgos et al., 2003; Dye and Espinal, 2001; Andersson and Levin, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Middlebrook and Cohn, 1953.

claim: It was hypothesized that drug-resistant MTBC-strains had a reduced capacity to transmit and would not widely disseminate in the general population.
source: Based on early observations that the acquisition of drug resistance could lead to reduced bacterial fitness (Middlebrook and Cohn, 1953), it was hypothesized that drug-resistant MTBC-strains had a reduced capacity to transmit, and would not widely disseminate in the general population (Borrell and Gagneux, 2009; Billington et al., 1999; Burgos et al., 2003; Dye and Espinal, 2001; Andersson and Levin, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous hypotheses.

claim: This optimistic scenario has been invalidated by abundant evidence for transmission of MDR and XDR-TB strains in healthcare and community settings.
source: This optimistic scenario has been invalidated by the now abundant evidence for transmission of MDR and extensively drug-resistant MTBC-strains (XDR-TB; MDR-TB additionally resistant to at least one fluoroquinolone and one injectable aminoglycoside) in healthcare and community settings (Borrell and Gagneux, 2009; Gagneux et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2013; Pym et al., 2002; Comas et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating MDR/XDR-TB transmission.

claim: In former Soviet Union countries, the expansion of drug-resistant MTBC-clones is thought to be promoted by interrupted drug supplies, inadequate implementation of regimens, lack of infection control and erratic treatment in prison settings.
source: In former Soviet Union countries, which experience the highest MDR-TB rates worldwide, the expansion of drug-resistant MTBC-clones is thought to be promoted by interrupted drug supplies, inadequate implementation of regimens, lack of infection control and erratic treatment in prison settings (Balabanova et al., 2004; Casali et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balabanova et al., 2004 and Casali et al., 2014a.

claim: Continued transmission is thought to be aided by the co-selection of mutations that compensate for fitness cost associated with rifampicin resistance.
source: Continued transmission is thought to be aided by the co-selection of mutations in the bacterial population that compensate for a fitness cost (e.g. growth deficit) associated particularly with the acquisition of rifampicin resistance mediating mutations (Borrell and Gagneux, 2009; Andersson and Levin, 1999; Gagneux et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2013; Pym et al., 2002; Comas et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on compensatory mutations.

claim: The compensatory mechanism for rifampicin-resistant MTBC-strains is proposed to be associated with structural changes in RNA-polymerase subunits RpoA, RpoB, and RpoC that increase transcriptional activity and enhance growth rate.
source: The compensatory mechanism for rifampicin-resistant MTBC-strains is proposed to be associated with structural changes in the RNA-polymerase subunits RpoA, RpoB, and RpoC that increase transcriptional activity and as a consequence enhance the growth rate (Comas et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Comas et al., 2012.

claim: The first cohort comprised 86% (49/57) of MDR-MTBC isolates from a cross-sectional drug resistance survey conducted in four districts in Karakalpakstan between 2001–2002.
source: The first cohort comprised 86% (49/57) of MDR-MTBC isolates from a cross-sectional drug resistance survey conducted in four districts in Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan between 2001–2002 (Cox et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cox et al., 2006.

claim: 228 isolates were obtained from TB-patients enrolled for second-line treatment in the MDR-TB treatment program from 2003 to 2006, representing 76% (228/300) of all MDR-TB cases diagnosed over the period.
source: An additional 228 isolates were obtained from TB-patients enrolled for second-line treatment in the MDR-TB treatment program from 2003 to 2006. These isolates represented 76% (228/300) of all MDR-TB cases diagnosed over the period.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study population description.

claim: The majority of isolates from both cohorts (69% and 64% respectively) were obtained from patients residing in Nukus.
source: While the MDR-TB treatment program covered two of the four districts included in the initial drug resistance survey, the majority of isolates from both cohorts, 69% and 64% respectively, were obtained from patients residing in the same main city of Nukus (Appendix—table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by demographic data from the study population.

claim: A 10 SNP-threshold was used to infer recently linked cases within a 10-year time period, based on MTBC genome evolution rate of ≈ 0.5 SNPs/genome/year.
source: This 10 SNP-threshold was used to infer the number of recently linked cases, as considered within a 10-year time period, based on previous convergent estimates of MTBC genome evolution rate of ≈ 0.5 SNPs/genome/year in inter-human transmission chains and in macaque infection models (Ford et al., 2011; Walker et al., 2013; Roetzer et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies establishing the MTBC evolution rate.

claim: 85.4% (622/705) of the MDR-MTBC isolates had the high-level isoniazid resistance mediating mutation katG S315T.
source: *The short MDR-TB regimen further includes high-dose isoniazid treatment, and clofazimine. In that regard, we identified 622/705 (85.4%) of the MDR-MTBC isolates with the well-known high-level isoniazid resistance mediating mutation katG S315T (Supplementary file 1), for clofazimine resistance mediating mutations are not well described.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: MDR outbreak strains already became resistant to both first- and second-line drugs in the 1980s.
source: Temporal reconstruction of the resistance mutation acquisition and of changes in bacterial population sizes over three decades demonstrates that MDR outbreak strains already became resistant to both first- and second-line drugs in the 1980s.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic reconstruction.

claim: Fully first-line resistant strains massively expanded in the 1990s, a period that shortly preceded or immediately followed the end of the Soviet Union.
source: Fully first-line resistant strains massively expanded in the 1990s, a period that shortly preceded or immediately followed the end of the Soviet Union, years before the implementation of DOTS and programmatic second-line MDR-TB treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic reconstruction and historical context.

claim: The expansion of fully first-line resistant strains in the 1990s is in line with the known rise in TB incidence that accompanied the economic breakdown in Russia during the 1990s.
source: This is in line with the known rise in TB incidence that accompanied the economic breakdown in Russia during the 1990s (Institute of Medicine Forum on Drug Discovery, Development, and Translation and Russian Academy of Medical Science, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Institute of Medicine Forum on Drug Discovery, Development, and Translation and Russian Academy of Medical Science, 2011.

claim: The acquisition of compensatory mutations after introduction of low fitness cost resistance mutations is the critical stage allowing for higher transmission rates.
source: The acquisition of compensatory mutations after introduction of low fitness cost resistance mutations (e.g. katG S315T (Pym et al., 2002), rpoB S450L (Gagneux et al., 2006), rpsL K43R (Böttger et al., 1998) seems the critical stage allowing for higher transmission rates.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data with citations to studies on specific mutations.

claim: Compensatory evolution appears to play a central role in driving large MDR-TB epidemics such as that seen with the Beijing CAO-clade.
source: Compensatory evolution thus appears to play a central role in driving large MDR-TB epidemics such as that seen with the Beijing CAO-clade.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple regression analyses and transmission data.

claim: High frequencies of mutations in the ribD promoter region and folC among Beijing-CAO isolates are a likely consequence of the use of para-aminosalicylic acid in failing treatment regimens in the late 1970s to the early 1980s in the Soviet Union.
source: For instance, high frequencies of mutations in the ribD promoter region, and folC among Beijing-CAO isolates, associated with para-aminosalicylic acid resistance (Zheng et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2014), are a likely consequence of the use of para-aminosalicylic acid in failing treatment regimens in the late 1970s to the early 1980s in the Soviet Union (USSR Ministry of Health, 1976; USSR Ministry of Health, 1983; Mishin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from resistance patterns with citations to historical treatment guidelines.

claim: The frequent independent emergence of mutations in the eis promoter and upstream region of whiB7 probably reflects self-administration of kanamycin that was available in local pharmacies.
source: Likewise, the frequent independent emergence of mutations in the eis promoter and of rare variants in the upstream region of whiB7, both linked to resistance to aminoglycosides (mainly streptomycin and kanamycin) (Zaunbrecher et al., 2009; Reeves et al., 2013), probably reflects self-administration of kanamycin that was available in local pharmacies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from resistance patterns with citations to studies on aminoglycoside resistance.

claim: The pre-existence of fully first-line resistant strain populations likely contributed to the poor treatment outcomes observed among MDR-TB patients following the implementation of first-line DOTS treatment in 1998.
source: The pre-existence of fully first-line resistant strain populations (e.g. CAO-Beijing in Karakalpakstan) likely contributed to the poor treatment outcomes observed among MDR-TB patients following the implementation of first-line DOTS treatment in 1998 (Cox et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from temporal data with citation to Cox et al., 2006.

claim: The period following DOTS implementation coincides with a detected CAO population size increase, likely reflecting the absence of drug susceptibility testing and appropriate second-line treatment.
source: This period coincides with a detected CAO population size increase, likely reflecting the absence of drug susceptibility testing and therefore appropriate second-line treatment during extended hospitalization at the time, resulting in prolonged infectiousness of TB-patients and further spread of these strains.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from population dynamics data.

claim: The frequencies of fluoroquinolone resistance remained low among Karakalpakstan MDR-MTBC isolates, consistent with the notion that such drugs were rarely used for treating TB in former Soviet Union countries.
source: The frequencies of fluoroquinolone resistance, mediated by gyrA and gyrB mutations, remained low among the Karakalpakstan MDR-MTBC isolates, which is consistent with the notion that such drugs were rarely used for treating TB in former Soviet Union countries (see Discussion (Casali et al., 2014a; USSR Ministry of Health, 1976; USSR Ministry of Health, 1983; Mishin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on data with inference supported by citations to historical treatment practices.

claim: The low fluoroquinolone resistance explains the generally favorable MDR-TB treatment outcomes observed with individualized second-line regimens including a fluoroquinolone in Karakalpakstan.
source: This observation explains the generally favorable MDR-TB treatment outcomes observed with the use of individualized second-line regimens, including a fluoroquinolone, in the latter MDR-TB treatment program in the Karakalpakstan patient population (Cox et al., 2007; Lalor et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from resistance data with citations to treatment outcome studies.

claim: Fluoroquinolone resistance is already emerging in Beijing clade A and B strains.
source: However, fluoroquinolone resistance, representing the last step towards XDR-TB, is already emerging as reported for strains in Beijing clade A and B (Casali et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Casali et al., 2014a.

claim: The pre-existence and wide geographic dissemination of highly resistant and highly transmissible strain populations most likely contributes to increasing M/XDR-TB incidence rates despite scaling up of MDR-TB programs.
source: In conclusion, the (pre-) existence and wide geographic dissemination of highly resistant and highly transmissible strain populations most likely contributes to increasing M/XDR-TB incidence rates despite scaling up of the MDR-TB programs in some Eastern European and Russian regions (Ulmasova et al., 2013; Institute of Medicine Forum on Drug Discovery, Development, and Translation and Russian Academy of Medical Science, 2011; Medecins Sans Frontiere, 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings with citations to reports on MDR-TB programs.

claim: Standardized therapies, including the newly WHO endorsed short MDR-TB regimen, are/will be largely ineffective for many patients in Samara and Karakalpakstan.
source: Importantly, from the large spectrum of resistance detected among dominating strains in this study, it can be predicted that standardized therapies, including the newly WHO endorsed short MDR-TB regimen in Uzbekistan, are/will be largely ineffective for many patients in Samara and Karakalpakstan, and likely elsewhere in Eurasia.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from resistance profile data.

claim: Universal access to rapid and comprehensive drug susceptibility testing will be crucial for guiding individualized treatment and maximizing chances of cure.
source: In order to successfully control the worldwide MDR-TB epidemics, universal access to rapid and comprehensive drug susceptibility testing, best supported by more advanced technologies, will be crucial for guiding individualized treatment with existing and new/repurposed TB drugs and to maximize chances of cure and prevention of further resistance acquisition.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings about resistance patterns and treatment implications.

claim: The pre-XDR rate among CAO isolates at the end of the study period in 2006 was 52.0% (90/173).
source: At the end of the study period in 2006, we observed a pre-XDR rate among CAO isolates of 52.0% (90/173), compared to 35.9% (23/64) among other Beijing isolates (p=0.03) and compared to 42.5% (17/40) among non-Beijing isolates (p=0.30) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by resistance profile data with statistical comparisons.

claim: The pre-XDR rate among other Beijing isolates at the end of the study period in 2006 was 35.9% (23/64).
source: At the end of the study period in 2006, we observed a pre-XDR rate among CAO isolates of 52.0% (90/173), compared to 35.9% (23/64) among other Beijing isolates (p=0.03) and compared to 42.5% (17/40) among non-Beijing isolates (p=0.30) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by resistance profile data.

claim: The pre-XDR rate among non-Beijing isolates at the end of the study period in 2006 was 42.5% (17/40).
source: At the end of the study period in 2006, we observed a pre-XDR rate among CAO isolates of 52.0% (90/173), compared to 35.9% (23/64) among other Beijing isolates (p=0.03) and compared to 42.5% (17/40) among non-Beijing isolates (p=0.30) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by resistance profile data.

claim: Only a single isolate was identified as harboring a gyrA mutation (A90V) associated with fluoroquinolone resistance.
source: Of note, only a single isolate was identified as harboring a gyrA mutation (A90V), associated with fluoroquinolone resistance (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: The DOTS implementation in Karakalpakstan in 1998 likely selected for CAO-strains, comprising 75% of sampled MDR-TB isolates in 2005/2006.
source: Introduction of standardized WHO-endorsed directly observed treatment, short-course in Karakalpakstan in 1998 likely selected for CAO-strains, comprising 75% of sampled MDR-TB isolates in 2005/2006.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal data showing increased CAO prevalence after DOTS implementation.

claim: CAO-isolates were identified in a published cohort from Russia (2008–2010).
source: CAO-isolates were also identified in a published cohort from Russia (2008–2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis of the combined dataset.

claim: The presence of mutations supposed to compensate bacterial fitness deficits was associated with transmission success and higher drug resistance rates.
source: Similarly, the presence of mutations supposed to compensate bacterial fitness deficits was associated with transmission success and higher drug resistance rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses showing associations between compensatory mutations and transmission/resistance.

claim: The genetic make-up of these MDR-strains threatens the success of both empirical and standardized MDR-TB therapies, including the newly WHO-endorsed short MDR-TB regimen in Uzbekistan.
source: The genetic make-up of these MDR-strains threatens the success of both empirical and standardized MDR-TB therapies, including the newly WHO-endorsed short MDR-TB regimen in Uzbekistan.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from resistance profile data showing high rates of resistance to drugs in the short regimen.

claim: The CAO clade dating back to 1974 subsequently acquired resistance mediating mutations to eight anti-TB drugs.
source: One clade (termed Central Asian outbreak, CAO) dating back to 1974 (95% HPD 1969–1982) subsequently acquired resistance mediating mutations to eight anti-TB drugs.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal phylogenetic reconstruction.
